utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours this is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Unfortunately we have a very late start due to the other Chamber taking more time without any consultation. We will try to be as efficient as possible to the extent. I'd also like, because it's the last day of Mr. Krajisnik's testimony to find an opportunity to regain the time perhaps by having a bit shorter breaks, absolute minimum, and perhaps with the indulgence of the interpreters and technicians to perhaps continue for another 10 or 15 minutes. It would save us from having an additional hearing tomorrow. Then very quickly, a few procedural matters. First, photographic evidence of the destruction, you are directed, Mr. Harmon and Mr. Tieger, to submit the photos including all supporting data as shown in, example, shown Excel spreadsheet attached to the 22nd of May e-mail, as well as the CD the Defence has given, until no later to the 29th to object.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got the CD. I've seen some of the photographs. Mr. Krajisnik is going to see the material. I'm going to need to speak to him about it. I do want the Defence to be in a position to object if we want to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I hope you don't hear it. We do hear which reminds me of dentists. I hope it's not your fate at the beginning of next week. And I would very much appreciate if it would stop. Then, Mr. Josse, if by Monday, you could not have made up your mind because you had no opportunity yet to speak to Mr. Krajisnik, then you can ask for --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He's going to need to see the material before I am in a position to know whether I wish to make any representations to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. If you find no possibility to see him before Monday, then we'll grant you a couple of additional days so that you have an opportunity to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I haven't seen the CD myself. We've only got one. I'll see if an extra one can be burned. There are some logistical problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The basic line is please respond as soon as possible, of course, after you have had a possibility technically also to discuss it with Mr. Krajisnik, after he has seen it, after you have seen it, try to be very practical.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two is the double pension legislation. The Chamber would like an immediate submission of the legislation. The matter has been discussed between the parties. But we would like to receive that legislation as soon as possible. As for --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no difficulty with that. I have just sent an e-mail on the subject to a legal officer but there is no difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have not seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've literally just sent it, Your Honour. But there is no difficulty submitting the material that we've got at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, counsel and I have conferred on this. He's going to make certain submissions as to portions of the legislation. I have portions of the legislation. I'm prepared to submit those right now, if the Court so wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The parties are invited to do it without further delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll do it at the next break, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Then P824 and related Official Gazettes, the OTP is invited to submit the documents available. That is the retranslation of P824, a decision on acquired rights based on tenancy rights and labour relations. And if available, submit Official Gazette 11-92 which contains the decree on the return to the Serb republic of the people who moved out. And in addition to that, you're invited also to submit Official Gazette 8-92 which contains the first printing of the decree - there was an error in it and it was then republished - so that we have all the material available. Then Mr. Josse and Mr. Stewart, I have one other matter to be discussed in private session. We'll do that at the end of this session. By the way, in the presence of Mr. Krajisnik. Who is going to continue the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm first off today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then, Mr. Krajisnik, although I'd forgotten to tell you not to speak with anyone about your testimony, I take it that you didn't do so and that you understood that that's a standard instruction and you are also standardly reminded that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just on that single point, may I say I associate myself precisely what Mr. Josse said yesterday on the issue of Mr. Krajisnik not being in court, including the recognition of the constructive and helpful spirit. It may never arise again, Your Honour. If it does arise again, we would particularly ask to be given notice because we, as Mr. Josse indicated, we don't feel comfortable with the principle that in practice, as far as yesterday is concerned, we have no more to say on the topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are going to ask straight away for a bit of the CD which is P70 to be played. That's the matter that Mr. Krajisnik mentioned yesterday and it's a different bit. It's all in evidence, Your Honour. There isn't a transcript of this bit that -- I'm informed but it's a very, very short clip so I hope that won't inconvenience anybody or it's a short --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see whether the interpreters can follow. If there is no transcript it might be a problem but --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "So that I at least do not know the name of the new Prime Minister designate. Question: There will be no more members of the Presidency of Republika Srpska, just the president of the Presidency and the president of the assembly is known. As we don't have a new Prime Minister designate or new members of the cabinet. Is this a new step in the functioning of the government of Republika Srpska in these new wartime conditions? Answer: I have to distinguish between two things here. One, there was an initiative and I don't know whether this will be realised although there is a good chance that it will be. In this time of war, we have to centralise the government and with a centralised government, create a state. That is how the idea came up, that from having a Presidency we should move over to a presidential system, to have a president, and this exists in our constitution because the presidency was just a transitional phase. I think the Presidency should remain, first of all, because three members of the Presidency, Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Koljevic and the president of the Presidency, Mr. Koljevic [as interpreted], are very active and important persons and are making a huge contribution to the Serbian people, and on the other hand, the people have accepted each of these as their own."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour, the -- must see -- Your Honour, we really couldn't do anything about the fact there isn't a transcript because this is in evidence but -- sorry, Mr. Harmon has got a --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm informed there is -- the transcript was put into evidence by the Prosecution, of this very portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of this part as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's P851.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In that case, I'm sure we can find that pretty quickly. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the portion that is referred to is found at page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I see, it came up during the evidence of Mr. Thompson. I should say Mr. Krajisnik was indicating to me that he wants to deal with point. Not entirely unreasonably. He did actually signal to me that he wanted to deal with the point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour has it. At the moment -- I'm sorry, we did understand in the preparations this morning that there wasn't a transcript. We are delighted to find there is. It's just I don't have it in front of me at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have it in front of me. If Mr. Krajisnik would like to add anything or make a comment on this --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Does Your Honour have an English transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have an English transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At some point, Your Honour, may I see it before I proceed with questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may have it because I have it double in front of me, both on my screen and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's kind, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the original so --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I won't make any paw marks on it, Your Honour. I'll hand it back pristine. I'm sorry, Your Honour, which page is it on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Page 4, thank you. Well, there was a certainly an ambiguity in the -- [Microphone not activated]. Your Honour, there was certainly an ambiguity in the English as interpreted for which I certainly don't blame the interpreters doing it off the cuff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask but it's a totally different matter, Mr. Registrar, the electronic copy jumps from uneven to uneven pages instead of covering it all, so I've now given away my one and only page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll give it back straight away, Your Honour. I don't -- thank you very much. That was very kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There isn't -- a question: Is there a B/C/S transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, is there a B/C/S? In hard copy that so that it could be presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It occurs to me Your Honour, if we put the B/C/S passage on the ELMO, then the interpreters and Mr. Krajisnik can see it, and then I think we are in business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Seems to be no B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: English is there. We have no B/C/S copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So it was translated straight to English? That's do you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe there is a B/C/S version but it's just not in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I tell you what, Your Honour, shall I move on and get my chaps to sort it out, Your Honour, so that we don't get bogged down on this, we can come back to it at the beginning of the next session or whatever. Otherwise, it's silly for us to get bogged down on these practical matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I agree. It's on the screen at the moment. If it --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, the B/C/S or the English? There isn't an English so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we could have it on the screen so if the interpreters need it and if Mr. Krajisnik would like to consult it, they are able to do so. So therefore could I instruct the technicians to show, and let me just now see --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I suppose the thing, Your Honour, would it be to just double check. Just this critical paragraph, just to ensure that the transcript matches what the interpreters or what everybody hears, the B/C/S speakers hear on the audio?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There we are. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, could you just read, please, perhaps from the second sentence of that passage that you see on the screen? You can start at about the 8th line. Well, we've lost the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Still further back, it's 23350, there we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We can start at the about the 8th line. Does it say [B/C/S spoken] it says, I'm told, reliably. Could you read out loud from there, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see -- I personally, if it's line 8, it's not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It starts with [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's line 8 of the passage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please assist --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, excuse me, I do see it now. "I personally think that the Presidency should remain. First of all, because three members of the Presidency, Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Koljevic, and the presidents of the Presidency, Mr. Karadzic, are very active and very significant persons, and are making a big contribution to the Serb people, on the one hand. Secondly, the people have accepted each one of these three members as their own, and they have their evaluation and so on." This is a comment -- may I?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You said "this is a comment," which is now you commenting today on that passage. This is a comment, Mr. Krajisnik. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was on the occasion of the assembly session of the 22nd of November in Zvornik, when an activity was initiated to introduce a president instead of a Presidency, and we had here the stenographic minutes of that meeting, where that quotation by Karadzic is explained. He said, when I'm not there, Mrs. Plavsic is there. When Plavsic isn't there, Koljevic is there. And when Koljevic is absent, Krajisnik is there. The conclusion that was drawn from this was that Krajisnik was a member of the Presidency. On the occasion of that initiative, I gave an interview on that day and in this interview I clearly stated who the members of the Presidency were. This interview was made because of that assembly session, not just the part that Karadzic spoke in but because of that initiative, to have a president. Later on, Mr. Karadzic was appointed president and the other two deputy presidents. And this change was introduced in December. You can see from this that I knew who the members of the Presidency were and that I was not one of them. That's why I am happy that this was read out. I've never seen this Serb translation, I have to say, nor have I seen this video before. I saw it for the first time only a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the way it -- the way we now have it, as the interpretation from your reading out of the transcript, in English, I appreciate you're going to get it back in your own language, but it says, first of all, because -- this is page 9, line 13, Your Honours, first of all, because three members of the Presidency, Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Koljevic and the presidents of the Presidency, Mr. Karadzic, are very active and very significant persons and are making a big contribution to the Serb people. Your Honours, the problem I have there is that's ambiguous in English, still. And I wonder whether it is ambiguous in the same way in Serbian on the original -- on the original disk. I see Mr. Tieger, I think agreeing that there is an ambiguity in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, just my recollection that there is always that problem with articles. So -- but it may again be something we need to check with the interpreters. I'm not sure it's best to do it again with the interpreters in court but we can have a more thorough check made.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it has to be done in this way, Your Honour, and there is no option but to raise the point fairly and squarely in English. Clearly if you say "the three members of the Presidency," it's saying those are the members of the Presidency whereas, if it says it without the definite article, it can imply something different. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask -- it's a very specific question. Could I ask the interpreters whether the portion just read by Mr. Krajisnik, where he says, "First of all because three members of the Presidency," whether it is in the original clear from the language itself, so not to draw any conclusions but whether the language leaves it open whether these are all three -- the only members of the Presidency, or whether the language would allow for an interpretation that there were more? It's about the article, as said by both Mr. Tieger and Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I observe, absolutely, Your Honour, may I observe in the end that if there is any possible difference it's going to be the language as used during the interview rather than strictly the language on the B/C/S transcript, because there's always the possibility that they do not match.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then first check that, whether the transcription is in this respect perfect. But then we have to replay it. By the way, these are matters that could be easily solved out of court, I would say, both in finding that there is a transcript, then with language assistance, the parties could agree whether the article or is how or whether the transcript is complete. But let's not lose any more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. We normally try to do that. I apologise. It's sometimes -- in this particular situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Stewart --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- when it came up, in the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, Mr. Stewart, I said let's proceed and not lose any further time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I just wanted to indicate why we apologise there is this difficulty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could that portion be played again? Only the couple of lines.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be a good thing to play it to the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course the interpreters could not see the transcript while listening. Could it be shown on the screen, the transcript now? The B/C/S transcript. Could the interpreters read from the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the interpreters heard -- heard the witness say "three," and because the definite article does not exist in B/C/S, this will always be ambiguous in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the transcript reflects what we hear on the video, and linguistically, the ambiguity will always be there?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's been clarified, Mr. Stewart. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you will have heard that. Do you have any -- well do you accept that as a matter of your own language, that ambiguity as to whether, when you refer to three members, you're meaning the only three members or three other possibly larger number of members is there as a matter of language?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is completely unambiguous here who the members of the Presidency are, and in the continuation, I keep talking about the characteristics of those three members, and I advocate that they remain. You can see from the entire text as a whole, and I know what I was saying. I also know who the members were. If you look at the further text, I say, it would be a pity if any of them were left out. I didn't say it would be a pity if any of us were left out. I'm advocating a three-member Presidency, those three members. I don't know how it is in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'm going to do with Your Honour's permission is move on, get all necessary bits of paper during the next break, have all necessary discussion with my B/C/S speakers in the next break, and then come back to it as necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, Mr. Stewart, it might be good to keep in mind that although certainly this is one part of the evidence and who was a member of the Presidency, that the Chamber, of course, will take into consideration every bit and piece of the evidence, not just the words used during an interview on who were members of the Presidency de jure, who were -- might have been members of the Presidency de facto, how it all functioned, what other witnesses said about it, what we find on paper about it, how to interpret having --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just pointing out to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We understand that, Your Honour. Very clearly we understand all that and have done for a long, long time, Your Honour. We do, though, recognise that Mr. Krajisnik is particularly concerned about this point and particularly concerned that he should not be understood, so -- not be misunderstood, so, Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's perfectly clear that Mr. Krajisnik told us now that the language he used in this interview should be -- that he considers that to support his view that he was not a member of the Presidency and linguistically, from what I understand, the opposite could not be concluded from the language used at this moment. But, of course, if further attention -- you'd like to pay further attention to it, you're free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll do it in the way I indicated, Your Honour, and not take my more time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I want to turn to a completely different topic, which is that yesterday afternoon, quite late on yesterday afternoon, you had referred to what was described as a brochure which was given the exhibit number D217, produced by the Ministry of human right and refugees for Bosnia-Herzegovina, that you were going to -- you have it there, I see, with you. You've got the pukka coloured printed version. You were going to have a look at that over night and, as I understood it, you were going to explain to the Trial Chamber what was particularly pertinent in this document. So please do.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is relevant is the first of these tables. In Serbian it bears the title, "Assessment of the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina based on the census of 1991."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that will be the one on page 4 of the English, I'm pretty sure, projection of population of BiH according to 1991 census. Yes, Mr. Krajisnik, we have that, I think.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to say at the end of this table, the expert commission looked at the municipalities of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the situation in 1991. Bosniaks, Croats and Serbs are listed here. I am drawing attention to the fact that out of 1 million 9 hundred and 56 thousand Bosniaks --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think the figure is gone wrong there, you're referring to 1.902.956, which is in the blacked out or highlighted band in the middle of page 7 of the English under the column "Bosniaks," towards the left. That's I think what you're talking about. So do continue, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said 1.902.956 Bosniaks lived in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Of these, 440.746 were in the present-day Republika Srpska. There is a map in front. This amounts to 23.6 per cent of all Bosniaks. I've left out the Brcko district here. The third column shows the Serbs. In the federation, there were a total of 1.366.104 Serbs. Of these, there were 478.122 in the federation. More nominally than there were Bosniaks in Republika Srpska. In terms of percentages, this accounts for 35 per cent. For the sake of illustration, in Republika Srpska, there were only 18 per cent Croats, 18 per cent of the entire Croatian population, that is. The rest were in the federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Pause there for a moment, Mr. Krajisnik. Your Honours at page 16 line 1 Mr. Krajisnik did say in the federation as recorded in the transcript but he clearly meant in the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I meant the federation. The total number in the federation was 478.122, so in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that's how many Serbs there were, and that's how many Serbs left the federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Krajisnik and it will be clear on any subsequent reading of the transcript so do continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to show that for 38.000, not the nominal figure, more Serbs left the federation and went to Republika Srpska and in percentage terms, the difference is 23.6 per cent. The number of Muslims who left Republika Srpska compared to 35 per cent Serbs who left the federation to go to Republika Srpska. And the total number of Croats, 18 per cent left Republika Srpska. I'm talking about the population displacement and movement. I'm not talking about expulsions, persecutions and so on. The second point that is essential that I'd like to point out is, and there are many facts and figures here, I don't want to abuse your patients but I would just like to indicate one more matter, and it is this. Table number 11 gives us the distribution of displaced persons in the year 2000 according to the municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Displaced persons, persons displaced by the war, but in the year 2000, I'm talking about how many people were displaced at that point in time. If you found the table, I can comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 22, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Displaced Bosniaks, 236.115 is the figure. Displaced Serbs, 2 [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 24 in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 267.752, which means that there were far more displaced Serbs here. And on the following -- in the following table, or rather graph, we can see the following: It says national structure or ethnic structure of the displaced persons in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as of the 30th of June 2003. Of all the displaced persons, 53.86 per cent were Serbs, and 43.91 per cent were Bosniaks. There were 8.77 per cent Croats. I have another piece of information here. Some more facts and figures. The household units privately owned according to the 1991 population census, table 12A --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right. So this is --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- housing units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Page 31 of the English. Yes, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosniaks, they had houses or housing units to the tune of 249.307 in the federation. 92.940 -- no, I do apologise. No. Yes, that's right. No. 177.656 were the number of units. I mixed things up. So the Bosniaks had 249.307 in the federation, housing units or houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's at page 33 of the English. It's about four items up in the column towards the left, headed Bosniaks. We are just trying to follow it, Mr. Krajisnik, because you've got one version and we've got another language version. Do continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do apologise. As I was saying the Bosniaks had 249.307 in the federation. And 93.939 in Republika Srpska. utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you just give me one second to follow along and find everything so that I better understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, Your Honour yes, the difficulty is, Your Honour, I can't easily interject those references without interrupting Mr. Krajisnik. When you said -- well, you haven't got the line 11 but where you say, "In the -- you say, as I was saying, it's line 8, as I was saying the Bosniaks had 249307 in the federation and 93.939 in Republika Srpska, the Serbs had the following," and you give the figures, "that means that an equal almost equal number of houses in Serbs in the federation and Bosniaks in Republika Srpska and the almost equal is the figure of 93939 in the 'Bosniaks' column and 92940 in the 'Serbs' column." utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What does that say, Mr. Krajisnik? I mean, you've given us a lot of figures. Before I start analysing it I'd like to know what conclusions you draw out of this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I want to do is to assist the Trial Chamber with respect to the population movement and displacement, and the property left behind by people when they moved. So that you can gain an impression and picture of how the Muslims -- what the Muslims and Serbs did. What the Serbs left on one sides and the Muslims on the other, how many Muslims left and how many Serbs left without entering into the conditions under which they left and moved, because this is the picture drawn by the professional services, without entering into whether it was ethnic cleansing or the free -- people who left freely. They are displaced persons today. And this is compared to the figures and the situation in 1991. Because the Serb population is lower, the percentages are far higher. It appears that far many Serbs left, there were far more housing units because there were 1.300.000 of one and 1.900.000 of the other and you can see who stayed on where and who left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether you can further analyse the figures, you have drawn our attention to and to see whether these would justify the conclusions, just to one thing that came into my mind, that the figures of the displaced persons might be influenced by the number of persons killed, for example, which would not be counted any more in 2000 because they have no place of residence any more so therefore I've got no idea what influence that would it have on the figures but at least it would be one element which from what I see now could not have been included in these figures, and therefore would have to be carefully considered before drawing statistical conclusions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I just ask something? It was my aim to show you that it would have been a good idea if a demographic expert had compiled this and presented the information. Now, Momcilo Krajisnik is the person who is saying this and telling you this. This is a surprise for me too. I just looked at the facts and figures and let me tell you that in the papers it was published that 120.000 -- there were 120.000 requests for property to be returned. They were requests to the federation made by Serbs, and 96.000 requests were sent into Republika Srpska by the Croats and Muslims for a return of property. So I'm talking about what the situation is like. Without saying whether somebody was expelled or not. I can't address that issue. As far as killings and other things are concerned, deaths and so on certainly that is the most important point because these people who have been displaced or moved out can return or need not return, whereas people who were killed have no chance of returning. So I understand that fully. This was just as far as displaced persons were concerned and I'm sure there is an another analysis on how many people were killed and who they were. But that wasn't the subject of this brochure and this was quite a surprise for me, too, because I didn't flow this is how things stood. So it would be a good idea if an expert were to compile this kind of report and then give us an explanation about what all these figures mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, could you be given, please, the document which is Exhibit P907, which is a demographic research report prepared by Dr. Ewa Tabeau and a colleague?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd just like to mention that I fulfilled my obligation to the president. I have brought in the minutes related to Deronjic, in addition to all the other documents that you have.

utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say it occurred to me earlier today that it is the position, really, that, as things stand at the moment, we would rather not have shorter breaks today, even if that causes a difficulty elsewhere, because Your Honour will see that today is a day when actually more than usually we need those breaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's on the record. We'll consider it. And please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, this document doesn't come as a complete surprise to you, that's apparent. It's been put into evidence and you have spent at least some time considering -- reading -- considering this document, report by Dr. Tabeau, have you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is quite correct. It is her report but I have to say that I didn't deal with it extensively. I didn't receive it on time and I didn't have enough time to go into it at any great length.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, in whatever time you --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I can answer your questions, of course. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'm delighted to hear that, Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Krajisnik, my first of all then, a general question: Do you have, then -- based on such reading and study of this report as you've been able to make, do you have any comment on it in relation to population movements in Bosnia and Herzegovina during not quite the same period as the report, during the period 1991 and -- particularly 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we had this report, I thought that we would have an expert on our side to reply and respond to Mrs. Tabeau. What I can say now, and it is my modest contribution, is this: She had a certain topic to deal with. She was not able to draw the conclusion as to when, during what time the displacement and movement took place, nor could she say under what conditions. But she did compile an analysis and I think it needs an expert to deal with properly. I consulted some experts and they consider that there are a lot of things that were not taken to fruition in this report, and that they were second hand information, if I can put it that way. Now, as far as the population displacement is concerned, there was general population displacement and movement in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I can say, of course, I don't know who was expelled and who left voluntarily so I don't want anybody to criticise me on that score but a large number of people did leave. They left their places of residence, wherever they were in the minority, whether in one way or another, because they considered that it wasn't their war, and all I can talk about is the Serb side. I can tell you why the Serbs moved, what I heard from them. I heard about the Muslim side for the first time here at the Tribunal, and, of course, through the media. But I heard from the Serbs themselves the reasons why they left, so if that can be helpful I can give you my impressions of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, let us look, for example, then, in this report, at 3.1. In the English it's on page 8. You of course have a slightly different version. It's page 7, top of page 7 of your copy, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have 3.1. 03083441 is the page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it begins it's the percentage of Muslims in the population of Krajisnik case municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that -- that's what you're looking at, are you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The text begins, "In the 37 municipalities included in the indictment," and that was the original number, it's dropped but it was 37. "In the 37 municipalities included in the indictment, the share of Muslims fell from 38.3 per cent in 1991 to 27.8 per cent in 1997, i.e., by 27.3 per cent." Those figures include all 37, though those assigned ultimately to Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and those assigned to Republika Srpska, after Dayton, and considering only the territories which eventually constituted Republika Srpska, the share of Muslims fell from 38 -- sorry, 31, my slip of the tongue, beg your pardon, 31.8 per cent to 1.4 per cent, i.e., by 95.7 per cent over the same period. And in the areas that in 1997 belonged to the federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the share of Muslims increased from 50.1 per cent in 1991 to 84.4 per cent in 1997. That's to say by 68.5 per cent. And then detailed figures by municipality are provided in table 1M in annex A. Mr. Krajisnik, I would like you to go to table 1M, please. It's in the English it begins at page 23. Well, I'm sorry begins actually at page 22 but in the English I'm going to page 24 where we deal with -- it's Sarajevo/Pale. Pale is under Sarajevo in that table. It's item 29 any way. The municipalities are given numbers. Do you find that, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is table 1NS, then that's Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, it's 1M. 1NS is an earlier table, Mr. Krajisnik. We get to 1M next?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 1M. I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's on page 22 of the Serbian version. Now, do you see the figures there are for Pale and they are divided up into the part of Pale which has fallen into the federation and the part of Pale which has fallen into Republika Srpska? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the comparison, of course, throughout Dr. Tabeau's report is between 1991 and 1997. And so far as the federation part of Pale is concerned, if I can call it that, the number of Muslims in that part of Pale was 963 in 1991 and had fallen to 369 in 1997, but, of course, we can see that at the same time there are no Serbs left there because the percentage has risen to 100, the Muslims 100 per cent of the population in that bit of Pale in 1997, and then the next line, in the -- what's now Republika Srpska bit of Pale, there were 2.658 Muslims living there in 1991 and only 10 recorded here as living there in 1997. Mr. Krajisnik, as best you can do, did those figures and that degree of change of the population in those two parts of Pale, are they consistent with your own knowledge and your own observations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say is this: And a lot of time has elapsed from my arrival to the end of the war, a part of Pale - Praca, it's called - came to belong to the Gorazde Muslim canton, and there was a church there on the side that came to belong to the Muslims, and the Serbs made themselves another church on the other side, but all the Serbs -- well, there weren't any more Serbs there, there were just Muslims there. So this division and the psychological division in Sarajevo, throughout Sarajevo, was like that. The people would go back to their canton even after the war. So I think this presents the proper picture. I don't know whether it's a good example for a proper picture. But it is the same picture that we see here. I don't know how many Muslims there are in Pale, whether 10 or five or 15. All I can do is say that I believe that there are 10, if it says so here but I didn't communicate with the ordinary man in the street about this, and I know that Praca, the area that belonged to the Muslim canton later on, the situation was like this. All the Serbs moved to Serb territory and left their church behind and their cemetery behind, and their graves, and so on. How they crossed, I don't know. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, anyway, Mr. Krajisnik, happily you've got the up to date one and we were looking at -- it was 20 -- page 24 of the English. We'll get to it, I think, Mr. Krajisnik, anyway, item 29, Sarajevo/Pale and my question, which I'm not sure to be honest, Mr. Krajisnik, that you had directly answered it, my question was whether those changes of population in the -- what is now the federation bit of Pale and on the other hand the Republika Srpska bit of Pale, are consistent with your own knowledge and observations of what happened in Pale from 1991 to 1997.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I learned, and I delivered a document, at the beginning of the war, before the Muslims left, all the Serbs were expelled. That's what they wrote in a letter to the municipality, from the Muslim part of Pale to Serb territory. It's in the documents I brought here. It's a letter presented to the executive committee of Pale with a request that accommodation be found for these refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, with the greatest respect that doesn't really go very directly to my question because your answer relates to all the Serbs having been expelled. The table we are looking at, at the moment relates to the changes in the Muslim population in the two bits of Pale. So I'm asking you whether the -- yes, it's page 22 of your version, whether those changes in the Muslim population are consistent with your own knowledge and observation in relation to the period 1991 to 1997.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood you to be asking about the Serbs from the Muslim part of Pale. If you're asking about the Muslims, I think the picture is as follows. As far as if heard. I don't have the precise information but I think that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And Mr. Krajisnik, if we then move on, and I'm going to invite Mr. Sladojevic to give the page number in your own version. It's at page 33 of the English. This is the equivalent table, it's 1S, it's equivalent table concerning Serbs and that's -- that's mentioned in the report itself, in the body of the report, at 6.1. If you like, they are matching sections of the report and that's the section major findings for Serbs whereas what we had looked at before was major findings for Muslims. I'm skipping over, Your Honours and Mr. Krajisnik, major findings for Croats and also major findings for others, not for any sinister motive, but, Mr. Krajisnik, if we then look at that table 1S, at page 22, wasn't it, it's Sarajevo/Pale, it's -- the specific item is on page 31, then, of your copy and we see again broken down in the same way Pale, FBH, federation, let's make sure we got the right point it says all ethnicities, do you see a figure 1.384? Do you see that figure?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Doesn't see that figure on their papers got the wrong paper. Then it's 407 Serbs, obviously the very precise number doesn't matter, Mr. Krajisnik, 407 Serbs in 1991 in that bit of Pale, none at all according to these figures in 1997, and then Republika Srpska bit of Pale, 9.195 in 1991 and that's grown to 12.866 by 1997. I haven't dwelt so much on percentages here but that's gone up to 95.6 so obviously it's really overwhelmingly most of the population. Again, Mr. Krajisnik, not the precise numbers, of course, but do those figures, do they accord with your own knowledge and observation of what happened in Pale between 1991 and 1997?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this must be approximately correct. A large number of Serb refugees left Pale, and I think this corresponds to the actual situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we got the 37 municipalities in this table that originally appeared in the indictment before a small number were removed so for practically purposes most of these indictments listed are still specifically identified and -- as the part of the Prosecution case on this indictment. Are there other municipalities on this list of which you would have, yourself, reliable knowledge from your own observation of the broad scale of population changes during the period 1991 to 1997? First of all, would that be true in relation to any of the Sarajevo municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just looking here, Novi Grad in Sarajevo. Well, in Rajlovac alone there were Serbs, but I see here that in the entire municipality, where there were about 30.000 Serbs, today there are only 2.000 something. As for Ilijas, this was a -- predominantly Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The question to start with then, Mr. Krajisnik, is do you have -- those two municipalities you've just mentioned, first of all, do you have at least a reasonable knowledge from your own observation of the scale of population changes as between the different ethnic groups over the period 1991 to 1997?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Novi Grad assembly, there were some Yugoslavs, but in the urban area, the majority were Muslims. However, I was commenting on the Serbs here because this is where there has been a reduction of the population. So that in Sarajevo, as a whole, one can see that in the Muslim part of Sarajevo, there has been a drastic reduction in the number of Serbs due to people moving out. I can comment on this by municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I inquire what we are listening to at this moment? It very much gives me the impression that you are drawing to our attention to the fact that the population movement in the other direction may have been of a similar size or even a bigger size than the moving out, I leave alone for what reasons, by Muslims. Is that a correct understanding or?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, it's not, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll further listen to what -- I don't know exactly, of course, it should not be said in the presence of the witness, what you are drawing our attention to but I wonder whether it is in dispute what -- but please think it over that it's not clear for me then. But perhaps it's also partly due to the answers given.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: They do come into the equation, Your Honour, you're absolutely right. And to some extent that's the answer to Your Honour's observation that what I am in a sense, of course, in asking questions I'm -- have in mind matters that will in some way be drawn to the attention of the Trial Chamber. But I'm in the hands of the answers as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that but because I think we started it with what was wrong with Tabeau's report, and apart from first of all the Tabeau report doesn't give a lot of answers to questions but is very much observing matters that happened with sufficient imprecision. I mean, she was not in a position to clearly make a difference between movement of population during the war, after the war, et cetera. There is a lot of information which is not in that report, and I think could not be in her report because of the data she had available to herself, and the -- I would say the rules of logic that -- the rules of her profession that she would have to apply. So please continue, then, and we'll -- hopefully we will understand what it actually is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe I can, I'll consider it. I believe I can help Your Honour more without saying something which ought not to be said in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm first of all just trying to establish -- and there need be no mystery about this. I'm trying to establish the degree to which Mr. Krajisnik, where he does have some knowledge of population movements, agrees broadly with what's in the Tabeau report. Because after all it's not my task or it's not in Mr. Krajisnik's interests to open up disputes where they don't exist. It's better to try to narrow them down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So that's what I'm trying to do first. Then, Your Honour, I am going to get, and there need be no mystery about there stated in broad terms I will go on to the questions in the area that Mr. Krajisnik can deal with but where, for exactly the reasons Your Honour indicated, Dr. Tabeau couldn't because she's an expert dealing with raw material and putting it together, not somebody who was there in 1991, 1992 and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Okay then. I think perhaps you could have gone more quickly to that point. I mean, I take it that you have spoken with Mr. Krajisnik. If there any point which he says this is not correct. But please continue. It's now clear to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you're heading for.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This is an area on which I have spoken to Mr. Krajisnik frequently, though not recently, Your Honour, except via the courtroom questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, so the particular municipalities that you mentioned a moment ago, it was Novi Grad, wasn't it, just so that I'm not getting mixed up about that. First of all it was Sarajevo/Novi Grad. I wanted to do it the same way, Mr. Krajisnik, but as quickly as we can, as I did before, by looking first at table 1M, I want to do Muslims then Serbs in that -- alphabetical order so -- give me the pages reference if you can, Marko. So Sarajevo/Novi Grad, appears on page 24 of the English and -- okay, and on page 22 of yours, you see?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The figures given there are that there were 55.789 Muslims living there in 1991, according to those figures. By 1997 that had become 44.413. Now, I'm leaving aside the overall population change for a moment, Mr. Krajisnik. We will come to aspects of that in a moment. But so far as the Muslim population of Sarajevo/Novi Grad, (federation), which identifies where it is, is concerned, is that consistent with your own knowledge and observations that there was a drop from 55 -- 56.000 or so in 1991 to around 44, 45.000 in 1997?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think the number has remained the same but the makeup has changed. Probably the other ethnicities are missing here because Novi Grad, as a municipality, is completely inhabited. There is no part of Novi Grad --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the other ethnicities are missing here except so far as they might be able to be inferred from the totals, just so there is no misunderstanding. This table is dealing with the changes of Muslims. The total population figures are given but this table deals with Muslims and there are separate tables dealing with the other ethnicities, we are going to come on to the Serb table at the moment. Do you see?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Novi Grad municipality is all in Muslim hands. There is no reason for the number of Muslims to have decreased. In fact, it has increased in Novi Grad because a large number of Serb territories now belongs to it and it's inhabited by Muslims, not Serbs. So I find this percentage surprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, is possibly -- I don't want to dwell on this particular point too long, is possibly the explanation of your reluctance to accept these figures that these figures relate to the change from 1991 to 1997 and, after all, time had moved on three years to the point where you were last in Bosnia and Herzegovina? You were there until 2000.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think these percentages and these numbers are correct. In 1996 when the Dayton Accord began to function, the Serbs left the area and the Muslim population increased, because a large number of Muslims moved into Serb ethnic areas. All of Rajlovac, for example, which used to belong to Novi Grad, and in the urban part of Novi Grad itself. For this reason, I think this piece of information cannot be correct by any means.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And if we go to table 1S, Mr. Krajisnik, page 33 of the English, that's item number 26, Sarajevo/Ilijas, it's page 31. Do you see that, Sarajevo/Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Is it 34 in my version?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 31, 31 in your version, Mr. Krajisnik. And it's number 26, they are always given the same numbers, I think, municipalities. Do you see there the --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see Ilijas, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay. The number of Serbs shown there in 1991, it's the second column of numbers, 9601, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And go on down in 1997 to 136. It might have been already tucked in one of your previous answers but is that consistent with your observations of what happened in that municipality over that period 1991 to 1997?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's an integral part of Sarajevo, and the Serbs left in large numbers, especially in 1995 and 1996. I don't know if there is 136 and something but I thought there was nobody there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, do you -- this report relates to 1991 to 1997, really apparently because of the raw material that was actually available. Do you have from your own observation knowledge of any municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina where a large number of Muslims left that municipality between 1991 and 1997?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be quite honest, I would have to review this in order to give you a proper answer. But if you tell me, I can tell you whether I think it's correct or not. I can comment on any examples you can give me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. Let's look, then, at table 1M, and Mr. Krajisnik, please understand here that I am -- I'm specifically looking, by looking at table 1M, just as Dr. Tabeau and her colleague are doing, looking at Muslims here and what numbers of Muslims left these municipalities during that period. Serbs are in a different table altogether. So are Croats and so on. We are not looking at those at the moment. Banja Luka, do you see number -- it's page [indiscernible] in the English and it's 1M. It's the first where 1M begins. It's page 20, okay?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours wish to pursue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So sorry, Your Honour, page 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Banja Luka, Mr. Krajisnik, 24.297 Muslims shown there, a distinct minority, clearly, but shown as living there in 1991 and by 1997, gone down to under 2.000. Do you know from your own observations of Banja Luka whether that is broadly correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 24.297. It's the second column.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that a larger number of Muslims remained and that there are more Muslims there than this figure would indicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But broadly speaking, Mr. Krajisnik, do you -- are you able to agree that the scale of movement out -- of Muslims from Banja Luka during that six-year period was from the 20-something thousands down to a very few thousand?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say quite truthfully that I cannot tell exactly how many have remained. I know that a contract was signed or agreement between Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Samaruga, and I don't know how many left and how many stayed. I couldn't tell you even an approximate number, but I know that there are many more there today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you yourself, Mr. Krajisnik, have knowledge of the scale of Muslim departure, if you accept there was such departure, from Banja Luka during the year 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only what I heard from Mr. Koljevic after the meeting. I didn't hear anything else. I didn't know how they left, but he told me that at one point he entered into an agreement with Mr. Samaruga of the ICRC and that a certain number of Croats left. As for other instances of people moving out, I was not informed of this. I wasn't aware of it. But as for this particular instance, I learned from him that a significant number of people left. This was towards the end of the war. Banja Luka had a large number of Muslims. I know that for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's go straight to number 14 on this list, Mr. Krajisnik, Gacko. Well, you can probably -- it's page 21, but we are just going down the numbered list now, Mr. Krajisnik, so a page number shouldn't figure a big deal. Have you got number 14, Gacko, in the same table?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Page 22 -- sorry, page 21, page 21.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Gacko, according to these figures, there were just over 3.000, 3.014 is the figure you see. Just over 3.000 Muslims in Gacko in 1991, and, by 1997, the number recorded is 4. Mr. Krajisnik, for working purposes, with all respect to those four, the Muslims had gone from Gacko. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what you know about how it was that the number of Muslims in Gacko went down from 3.000 to, for all practical purposes, none at all, over that six-year period?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know for Gacko is this: When the Muslims left, the deputy said at one point that they wanted to go, that they put in a request to leave, and showed a document, and I think the Trial Chamber has it, and the Prosecution does too, where the SDA Executive Board had asked them to go. Now, allegedly after that, the SDA said that they distanced themselves from that document. They weren't in the town themselves. They were in Fazlagica Kula, which is a settlement a little out of town, and after that they left and went to Montenegro. So that's the story that reached me, after some time. That's what I know about Gacko, that they had left and asked to leave and also were given instructions to leave. That's the only town in Herzegovina that I know about, having talked to someone with respect to their departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then Kalinovik, the next one, there were just over 1.000, 1156 recorded here in 1991 and three, Mr. Krajisnik, so the same comment applies as previously, do you know how it was that the number of Muslims in Kalinovik went down from 1156 to 3 or for practical purposes, the Muslims had gone by 1997?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although there was a deputy from Kalinovik, I never heard from him, nor did I discuss how the people from Kalinovik left, nor did I know that they had left. The only thing that I did hear about was on the 12th of May, at an assembly of the Serb people held in Banja Luka, that Mr. Mladic, who originates from those parts, said that he was, together with a government member, that he went there by helicopter and that he guaranteed them all their rights and freedoms and safety, and that he had a very positive meeting. And after that there were no further -- there was no further information about that small town. I had no further information about that small town.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right. Now, unless you have something special to add about Nevesinje, Mr. Krajisnik, it's right next to Kalinovik and Gacko, and in the interests of time I'm into the going to ask you about that. Unless you say there is something special, I'm going to move on to Prijedor, number 19, because that is after all in a completely different part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In Prijedor, there are 40.075 Muslims shown as living there in 1991. By 1997 the figure has gone down to 397. Are you able to tell the Trial Chamber what you know about how it was that around 40.000 Muslims, according to these figures, left Prijedor during that period?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When this process was going on, I had no information at all about it. But in the period after that, I received the following information: That an agency, transport agency existed, which before the armed conflict had taken a large number, predominantly Muslims, out of Prijedor, and this -- a statement to that effect was made by one of the participants, or, rather, a potential witness who was then deputy in parliament. The second point is this: I heard, once again subsequently, when journalists came visiting, when they came to visit Prijedor, that a certain number of them had been taken prisoner, a certain number of people had been taken prisoner and then the camp was disbanded. And they said clearly, and I said that here, that there was a collection centre and that prisons existed as well, and they were allowed to visit them quite freely. And the warden of Trnopolje prison gave a statement, he has died since but you can see the statement which confirms that it was a collection centre and he describes everything that went on there. So I learned all this later on, when I came here. What --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, I know it's late in the period of examination but I feel I should urge a reminder again that we -- that Mr. Krajisnik be asked to refrain from references to statements that are not in evidence and that may not be in evidence. And I understand that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's totally impossible for us to seek any verification. Apart from Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Stewart, I just draw your attention to it, is -- in rather general terms tells us what happened in what he calls a collection centre which is the subject of quite a number of adjudicated facts. So therefore, it would need a more thorough attack on those adjudicated facts to get them off the record. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's -- well that's certainly understood by us, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we are concentrating on the -- what you know about the, according to this report, reduction -- very large reduction in the Muslim population in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood it that I was supposed to tell the Trial Chamber everything I knew about this, and one of the things that I did know came from a statement that was not in this case, from somebody who died, and I'm sure the president will remember when I said that I'd learnt from my contacts that Trnopolje was a collection centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, if there is an adjudicated fact, it means that the Prosecution doesn't have to prove that any more because it has been thoroughly looked at by another Trial Chamber. There is nothing that would prevent you from leading evidence which would come to a totally different conclusion. Nothing would preclude you from --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But just referring to a statement of someone who died as one single element where this finding is based upon a couple of months of thorough litigation, really makes no sense. Again, a full attack, it's certainly something you could have done, but just to make reference to statements we do not have adding one little element, really makes no sense. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Krajisnik; Mr. Stewart, I allow him now to continue the questioning. If there would be anything at the very end of your testimony you would like to say but it seems to me, but, of course, I may be wrong, that you do not fully understand the procedural context in which you gave these answers. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'll try and help by putting a slightly different question, then. By the end of 1992, what did you know about how it was -- well, I better preface this by saying the Tabeau report deals with the period 1991 to 1997, let's bear that in mind, but by the end of 1992, what did you know about any reduction of the Muslim population of Prijedor and, if there was such a reduction that you knew about, how it had happened?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any knowledge about any reduction in Prijedor. I even attended an assembly meeting but we didn't discuss that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you know anything about killings in -- of Muslims in Prijedor during 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that from the report that was tabled by the journalists, and there is a document that I wanted to highlight or rather documents that speak differently, I learned there that there was a quite different picture than was painted to the public. So the picture was that it wasn't a camp, concentration camp, killing, well, that's the impression I gained and the picture I gained from those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, again I'm not going to ask you about the next one, Prnjavor, number 20, because we just do have limited time for everything really. Number 21, Rogatica, do you see that, on the list in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I ask you something, if that's not a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it's not conventional but sometimes it helps from a practical point of view, through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will listen to your question and then we'll see if it's appropriate to put such a question to counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm interested, and I talked to my lawyer or counsel, does he mean to override adjudicated facts such as Trnopolje, et cetera? We have a lot of documents, not just one document. If he doesn't intend to do that, then I don't see the reason for this. I don't know whether it's correct. I just wanted to present it as being something opposite to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not think that Mr. Stewart should at this moment answer that question, but it's clear that it's something that came into my mind as, and that is: Whether, and by what means, it should be considered to challenge adjudicated facts. That's a question that came into my mind. Well, Mr. Krajisnik, I do understand that it has come to your mind as well. I'm not interfering in any way in what Mr. Stewart does at this moment. We leave it to him. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I just was going to ask you about Rogatica. I just wanted first of all, please, to make sure that --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No apology needed. The -- item 21, still on page 21. Rogatica, the figure shown for Muslims living there in 1991 is 10.851, and in 1997, 3. Mr. Krajisnik, I'm going to put a slightly different form of question in relation to Rogatica. What do you know, Mr. Krajisnik, if anything, about how much, if any, of such a large population change of Muslims as is shown in this report had occurred by the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about population movement in 1992, from Rogatica, but the criticism I can make is that I know that there are at least more than three Muslims from the contacts I've had with the Serbs, so that I find it very surprising that there should be only three Muslims in Rogatica as recorded here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, this was three in 1997. I respectfully suggest, unless we are talking about dramatically different figures from the three, can we concentrate on my question, which is what you --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: For the -- what had happened by the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I didn't know how the Muslims came to leave. Later on, from contacting people, or rather from my contacts with people, I don't want to mention that they gave statements or anything like that, I was told that they wished to leave because the municipality was divided. So the Serbs were expelled first and then, allegedly after that, the Muslims left and went to Gorazde but I learned that after the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we go to number 32, Sokolac? It's on page 24 of the English and page 22 in your copy, Mr. Krajisnik. And you see there the number of Muslims recorded as living in Sokolac in 1991 was 4.250 and only two recorded as being there in 1997. Again, Mr. Krajisnik, up to -- what do you know about the scale, if any, of Muslim -- reduction of the Muslim population in Sokolac by the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I have no information about the Muslims. And let me explain about the Muslims departure. I didn't know that there were any Muslims in the small town itself. There is a settlement quite a long way away from Sokolac called Knezina, so probably that number of Muslims lived over there. I never talked to anybody about the departure of Muslims from that area, from the area of Sokolac, nor do I know under which conditions they left. When I came here, and when people testified, that's when I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And can we look at Visegrad, which is number 35? Should be on the same page but it's just a few items down. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 11.178 Muslims shown as living in Visegrad in 1991, and in 1997, this report says only three. First of all, I'm going to go back to that period 1991 to 1997. First of all, Mr. Krajisnik, are -- do you have any knowledge yourself which enables you to accept or disagree with the scale of the figures shown in this report for that change in population of Muslims in Visegrad over that six-year period?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely, the number of Muslims has dropped. Not only dropped but this report is probably quite close to the truth. There is just one thing that I learnt from reading the newspapers, and that is that a m mosque was built there and that a number of people returned. How many, I don't know. I don't know how many returned, whether they actually did return, but that the Muslims left is Visegrad en masse that was true although as I say I didn't know that at the time. I learnt this on one occasion after I went to Visegrad, to a Spa there after the war and I know that there weren't any Muslims there. But how they came to leave, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you say you didn't know that at the time, can we be clear what time it is that you're talking about that you now believe they left?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992. I didn't know in 1992. You've already asked me that, if I understood you correctly. In 1992, I did not know under what conditions the number of Muslims were reduced and in what way they came to leave Visegrad. What I remember now, and what I omitted to say is this: There was a telephone conversation between General Kukanjac and a man called Sabanovic, where Mr. Izetbegovic participated. The war had begun and he was asking for the withdrawal of the JNA, et cetera, and all that was not to blow up the dam. But I don't know how the Muslims left or whether they left or how they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, the last one on the list is Zvornik. But what I want to do with Zvornik is ask you to look, please, at both the Muslim figures in table 1M and the Serb figures in table 1S. Mr. Krajisnik, I can give you another copy of the report you've got so that you can have the two pages alongside each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the pages in the English are 24 and 33. And what I'm handing to you opened to page 31 has the 1S table so it's got Zvornik for 1S. So you can put that alongside the Zvornik figures in table 1M. Do you see? Just so we make sure we've got the right documents, 1M, the bottom figure in the left-hand column on the page you're looking at should be 53760. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay. Well I'm sorry it's actually the same figure on the other page as well. The one next to it should be 29452. Immediately to the right should be a figure 29452. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The other page 1 S the figure should be 22535; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Good, we got the right pieces of paper, Mr. Krajisnik. So now, do you see that on 1M -- well, Zvornik, first of all, is divided in here into two sections. That bit of Zvornik, Sakanovic [phoen], fell into the federation eventually, and that bit called Zvornik which fell into Republika Srpska. You see that and you agree that's what happened?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
